store.0: I'm a Computer Science major, and I'm in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is really packed, but it's a good kind of busy. I'm finally taking the higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to for a while. It's surreal to be at this stage, looking back on how far I've come. It feels like just yesterday I was in an intro class learning about simple data structures, and now I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even quantum computing basics. It's exciting to see how much I've grown and how much more I have to learn.
store.1: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm a huge fan of theory when it connects directly to real-world problem-solving. I find it fascinating to explore how we can optimize pathfinding in large networks or handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. The class covers everything from dynamic programming approaches to approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It can be mind-bending at times, but in a good, challenging way. Our professor is great at explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll present a seemingly impossible problem on the board and then show us a strategy to approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing with ideas and insights.
store.2: I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is probably the second hardest. It's a lot of reading, group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. We have to collaborate with people who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas about what the final product should look like. However, that's also the beauty of it. In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle issues like concurrency and node failures. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we fixed that and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.
store.3: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take for me. The professor is actually from the industry; he worked on a couple of indie games that got some decent traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, how to implement physics, and even a bit of user experience design. It's unbelievably fun because every assignment is super creative. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, and it was all about balancing the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. Getting that design right was tricky, but it was also rewarding to see it come together.
store.4: I also have to mention my Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which I initially thought might be a bit intimidating. However, the professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than just pure math. Of course, there is math involved, like linear algebra, but it's interspersed with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers, but we're modeling basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they theoretically outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff and has made me rethink how I approach problems.
store.5: My Capstone Project course is definitely the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group and I decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It's a fancy-sounding project, but essentially, we're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts by analyzing tweets or posts for words that suggest a disaster or crisis. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major, including database management, building an API, front-end interface, and the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to keep ourselves organized. One person on our team is the designated "Scrum Master," so each week we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all that agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.
store.6: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind, which is my last required non-CS elective. I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss topics like consciousness, the concept of mind, and how they might apply to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of class discussions, which is a nice change of pace from all the coding in my other classes. It's great to take a step back and analyze abstract ideas. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, such as the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was a fascinating experience. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for this perspective.
store.7: My schedule is pretty typical for a college student. Mondays and Wednesdays are the busiest days. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be tough if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do some undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload. I'm just trying to stay organized and make the most of my senior year.
store.8: The biggest challenge this semester is definitely balancing the group projects. The Capstone Project alone can consume around ten hours a week, and it can easily go up to more if we encounter any major bugs or if the model isn't training properly. Additionally, the Distributed Systems project is another significant time sink. My group tries to meet at least twice a week to discuss progress and coordinate our efforts. We also rely heavily on Slack or Discord to keep each other updated and share information. Coordinating five different people's schedules can be a mini-nightmare, but despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic and focused on learning, without the pressures of an actual job environment. It's a great opportunity to apply everything I've learned and make the most of my senior year.
store.9: I'm having a blast this semester! I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but now I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, but it's not as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, how to collaborate, and how to think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a pretty great feeling.
